paragraphs.text: Sermon on the passage of the Gospel: "Inasmuch as you did it to one of these," and what follows. I am still held by the sight of the King's fearful appearing, which the Gospel describes. My soul still cowers as it gazes on the terror of what was said. In a way it seems to see the King of heaven himself, as the passage says, seated fearfully on the throne of glory; and that magnificent throne, whatever that throne may be which contains within itself the one who cannot be contained; and those countless myriads of angels standing in a circle around the King; and the great and fearful King himself, bending down from his ineffable glory toward human nature, gathering to himself the whole race of human beings, from the time there first were human beings until that fearful appearing, and bringing judgment on each according to the worth of the life they have lived. On those who have lived by a right choice he bestows, as it is said, the things of the right hand; to the perverse and the reprobate he allots the sentence that fits the lives they have led. And he pronounces over each group: to the one that sweet and good word, "Come, you who are blessed by my Father"; to the other that dreadful and fearful threat, "Depart, you who are cursed." My soul has been so affected by the terror of what was read that I seem to be in the very presence of these events and to perceive nothing of what is around me, and my mind has no leisure to look at anything else among the matters set before us for examination and contemplation in the passage. Yet these are no small questions, nor worthy of only a little inquiry: how it is that he who is always present is said to come. For he says, "Behold, I am with you all the days." And if we believe that he is with us, how can he promise to come as though he were not present? For if

we live and move and have our being in him, as the Apostle says, there is no way that he who holds all things in his grasp could be separated in place from those who are held within him, so that we should suppose him not present now to those he encompasses, or expect that he will be present at some later time. And what is the seat of the bodiless one? What is the appearing of the invisible one? What is the [?] of the one who has no shape? What is the circumscribing on a throne of the one who cannot be contained? All such questions I will put aside, since they are too great for the present occasion. Instead, as far as I am able, I will turn my discourse to our common profit: how we may avoid being thrust into the ranks of the reprobate. For I am terrified, brothers, greatly terrified at the threat, and I do not deny what my soul feels. I would wish that you too did not hold these fears in contempt. For "blessed is the one who fears all things out of reverence," and "he who despises a matter will be despised by it," as the word of Wisdom says somewhere. Let us therefore take care, before the hour of evils arrives, that we do not come to experience those grim things. And what is the way of escape from what is fearful? To choose that way of life which the Gospel has just now shown us, the one truly fresh [?].

And what is the way? "I was hungry, I was thirsty, I was a stranger, and naked, and sick, and in prison. Inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me." And for this reason, he says, "Come, you who are blessed by my Father." What do we learn from this? That care for the commandments is a blessing, and negligence about the commandments is a curse. Let us love the blessing and flee the curse. For it lies with us to choose either one or not, as we have the power; whatever we incline toward with our desire, in that we shall be. Let us therefore make our own the Lord of the blessing, who counts as done to himself the zeal shown toward those in need—and especially now, when in this present life the commandment has so much material to work on. Many lack the necessities of life; and many lack even their own bodies, wasted away by a cruel disease. Let us therefore, through our zeal toward these, secure for ourselves the good promise. I mean plainly those who have been mutilated by the grievous disease. For the greater their sickness, the greater, clearly, the blessing for those who accomplish the laborious part of the commandment. What then must we do? Not oppose the ordinance of the Spirit. And this is: not to estrange ourselves from those who share our nature, and not to imitate those men who are condemned in the Gospel—I mean the priest and the Levite, who pitilessly passed by

that man in need of mercy who, the story says, had been left half-dead by robbers. For if they were blameworthy for not turning to look at the wounds swelling on his naked body, how shall we be free of guilt if we imitate the blameworthy? And yet what was there to see in the man who had fallen among robbers that compares with the sight of those who have been seized by this disease? You see a human being reshaped by this cruel sickness into the form of a four-footed beast, putting pieces of wood under his palms in place of hooves and claws, and leaving a strange track on the roads of men. Who would recognize from the track that it was a human being who had stamped such marks on the way? A human being, upright in form, who looks up to heaven, who has hands given him by nature to serve in his works—this one is bent to the earth, becomes four-footed, and falls little short of being a brute beast. With rough and rasping breath he groans violently from deep within his innards; or rather, if one may dare to say it, he becomes even more wretched than the brutes. For they, for the most part, keep the form they were born with to the end, and none of them is changed into some other form by any such misfortune. But this man, as though his nature had been altered, appears to be something else, and not the familiar living creature. His hands take over the use of feet; his knees become his base of support; while his natural supports, his feet and ankles, either drop off altogether or are dragged along at random, hanging loosely like something extraneous towed behind. When you see a human being in such a state, do you not respect your kinship? Do you not pity one of your own race? Do you instead loathe the misfortune and hate the suppliant, shunning his approach as though it were the attack of a wild beast? Yet you ought to reflect with a grateful heart that an angel touches you, a human being, and though he is bodiless and immaterial, he did not loathe one who is compounded of flesh and blood. But why do I speak of angels? The Lord of the angels himself, the King of heavenly blessedness, became a human being for your sake, and clothed himself with this foul-smelling and filthy flesh, together with the soul bound up in it, so that by his own touch he might heal your afflictions. And you, who share the same nature as the sick man, flee from one of your own kind? No, brother, do not let this evil counsel please you. Know who you are and about whom you are deliberating: that you are a human being deliberating about human beings, possessing nothing peculiar to yourself apart from our common nature. Do not pronounce in advance on what is to come. For when you condemn the affliction while it still appears in someone else's body, you pass an unrestricted sentence against the whole of nature—and you share in that nature just like everyone else. So let us speak of it as a matter that concerns us all.

Why then does no pity come over you at what you see? You see human beings wandering like grazing cattle, scattered about in search of food. Rags wrapped around them—that is their clothing; a staff in their hands—that is their weapon, that is their vehicle, and not even held in their fingers but tied to their palms with straps. A torn bag, and a crust of bread spoiled with mold and rot: their hearth, their house, their bedding, their couch, their storeroom, their table, all the furnishing of their life—it is the bag. And then you do not consider who it is that lives in this state? That it is a human being, made in the image of God, appointed to rule the earth, having the service of the brute beasts under his hand—and he has come to such a pitch of misfortune and change that what one sees is ambiguous, bearing on itself clear marks neither of a human being plainly nor of any other living creature. If you liken him to a human being, the human form disowns such shapelessness; if you turn the comparison to the brutes, they too will not accept the likeness of what you see. Such people look only to one another, and herd together because their sufferings are alike. They are loathsome to everyone else, but out of necessity they do not loathe one another. Shut out from everywhere, they flock together and become a people of their own. Do you see these joyless dancers, this mournful and gloomy chorus? How they parade their own misfortunes! How they put nature on show in themselves in its disfigurement, like conjurers displaying their manifold diseases to those who gather around! Composers of mournful laments, songwriters of those wretched songs, tragic actors of this empty and unhappy tragedy, who do not use borrowed tragedies for their sufferings but fill the stage with their own evils. What postures! What tales! And what do we hear them say? How they were driven out by their own parents for no wrongdoing; how they are banished from public gatherings, from feasts and festivals, like murderers or parricides condemned to perpetual exile—or rather far more wretched even than they. For murderers may at least move elsewhere and live among human beings; but these alone of all people are shut out from everywhere, as though they had been declared common enemies, judged unworthy of a shared roof, a common table, or the use of utensils. And that is not yet the worst: not even springs flow for them in common with other people, nor are rivers trusted not to carry along some of the pollution of the disease. If a dog laps the water with its bloodied tongue, the water is not thought loathsome because of the beast; but if the sick man comes near the water, at once the water too is condemned because of the man. These are the things they recount, these the things they lament; and so the wretched people are forced to throw themselves in the path of others, becoming suppliants of everyone who happens by. Many times I have wept at this grim sight; many times I have been indignant with nature itself; and now, at the

memory, I am overwhelmed. I have seen a pitiable affliction; I have seen a sight full of tears. Human beings lie along the roads in the path of passers-by—or rather no longer human beings, but the wretched remains of what were once human beings, needing tokens and signs to be believed to be such. For they cannot be recognized as human from the features of their nature. They alone of all people hate themselves; they alone curse the day of their birth—and with reason they hate that day, which began such a life for them. They are human beings who are ashamed even to call themselves by the common name, lest by sharing the name they should disgrace our common nature through themselves. They live with constant groaning, having an unceasing reason for lament. For as long as they look at themselves, they always have cause for mourning, at a loss over what to bewail more: the parts of the body that no longer exist, or those that remain; what the disease has already consumed, or what is left for the disease; that they see such things in themselves, or that they cannot even see, their sight having been darkened by the affliction; that they have such things to tell about themselves, or that they cannot even tell their sufferings, having been robbed of their voice by the affliction; that they live on such food, or that the disease does not let them take even that easily [?], since the corruption of the parts around the mouth hinders eating; that they suffer the lot of the dead while still able to feel, or that they have been robbed of their very senses as well. For where among them is sight? Where is smell? Where is touch? Where are the rest of the senses, which the rot devours as the affliction spreads little by little? For this reason they roam through every place, moving on like the brutes in search of richer pasture, carrying their misfortune about as their provision for trading for food, and holding out their disease to everyone in place of a suppliant's olive branch. They need others to lead them by the hand because of their sickness, and in their helplessness they prop one another up. Each is weak by himself, but they become a support for one another, using each other's limbs in place of those they lack. For they do not appear one by one; even wretchedness has a certain wisdom in devising a way to live—namely, that they wish to be seen together. Each of them is pitiable on his own, but in order to make people more compassionate they become an addition to one another's suffering, contributing to this wretched common fund, each collecting pity for them all through his own particular misfortune. One holds out mutilated hands; another displays a swollen belly; another a ruined face; another a rotting leg; and another bares whatever part of the body it may be and shows the affliction there. What then? Is this enough to keep us from transgressing at all against the law of nature: merely to recite the sufferings of nature in tragic style, to dress up the disease in words,

and to be moved at the memory of it? Or do we also need some deed that shows compassion and fellow-love toward such people? For what a shadow-painting is to real things, that is what words are when divorced from deeds. The Lord does not say that salvation lies in speaking, but in doing the works of salvation. So we must ourselves take up the commandment concerning them. Let no one say that it is enough to supply food to them after they have been settled somewhere far from our own life, on some remote frontier. Such a view shows no mercy or compassion; it is rather a plausible-looking scheme for banishing these people from our life altogether. And then, are we not ashamed of our own way of life, when we keep pigs and dogs under the same roof with us? Often the hunter does not even keep his puppy out of his own bed. The farmer knows how to greet his calf with a kiss. And that is not yet much: the traveler washes his donkey's feet with his own hands, puts his hand in to clear away the dung, and looks after its bedding. Yet the one who shares our kind and our race—shall we treat him with less honor than the brute beasts themselves? Not so, brothers, not so! Let this sentence against human beings not be ratified. It is fitting to remember who we are and about whom we are deliberating: that we are human beings deliberating about human beings, having nothing peculiar to ourselves apart from our common nature. There is one entrance into life for all; one way of living for all, eating and drinking; the activity of living is alike; the constitution of our bodies is one; and the end of life is one—every composite thing comes to dissolution. Nothing that has been put together has a permanent structure. Like a bubble, the body is wrapped around our breath for a little while, and then we are extinguished, leaving behind in the world no trace of this passing puff of air. Our memorials are in pillars and stones and inscriptions, and not even these last forever. So, reckoning these things in your own case, "Do not be high-minded," as the Apostle says, "but fear." It is uncertain whether you are not laying down this harshness as a law for yourself. You flee from the sick man, tell me? What charge do you have against him? That the moisture in him has been corrupted, and some putrid humor has been sown in his blood, black bile having been poured into the fluid? For this is what one hears from physicians when they explain the natural causes of diseases. What wrong, then, has the man done, if nature, being a fluid and unstable substance, has slipped into this kind of sickness? Do you not see in healthy bodies too that someone who is otherwise in good condition often suffers a blister, or a carbuncle, or some such affliction, when the moisture in that part becomes overheated beyond what is proper and so suffers inflammation and redness and a kind of purulent corruption? What then? Do we make war on the sick part of our flesh? On the contrary, we turn all the healthy part of the body to the care of the part that is diseased. So it is not the affliction that is loathsome. Otherwise, in our own case too, when one part was in pain, the healthy part would have kept itself apart from the

care of the part that was suffering. What, then, is the cause that keeps us away from such people? What is it? It is that we do not fear the threat of him who said, "Depart from me into the eternal fire; for inasmuch as you did not do it to one of these," he says, "neither did you do it to me." If people believed that these things were really so, they would not hold such an opinion about the sick as to drive them away from themselves and to think that zeal for the wretched is a defilement of our life. So, if we believe that he who made the promise is trustworthy, we must take hold of the commandments, without which it is impossible to be found worthy of what we hope for. A stranger, naked, lacking food, sick, and shut in—this man is all of these for you, everything that was mentioned before in the Gospel. He wanders about as a vagrant and naked; naked, and lacking necessities as well, because of the poverty that follows upon his affliction. For one who has nothing of his own at home and cannot work for hire is necessarily without the means of living. And he is a prisoner, fettered by his sickness. So in these people you have the whole fullness of the commandments being fulfilled, and the Lord of all himself becoming your debtor through your kindness to such a one. Why then do you strive against your own life? For to be unwilling to have the God of all dwelling with you is nothing other than to become a powerful enemy against yourself. As he comes to dwell with us through the commandment, so he is separated from us through harshness. "Take my yoke upon you," he says; and by "yoke" he means the practice of the commandments. Let us obey the one who commands; let us become Christ's beasts of burden, binding ourselves with the straps of love. It is light; it does not chafe the neck of the one who goes under it, but makes it smooth. "Sow bountifully," says Paul, "so that you may also reap bountifully." A rich ear of grain will spring up from such sowing. The crop of the Lord's commandments—the yield of the blessing grows tall. Do you want to learn how high the growth of the yield reaches? It touches the very heights of heaven. For whatever you do for these people, you bear fruit for the treasuries of heaven. Do not despair of what is said; do not think the friendship of such people something to be despised. The hand has been mutilated, but not for giving aid. The foot has been crippled, but it is not prevented from running toward God. The eye has wasted away, but through the soul it sees the good things that cannot be seen. So do not look at the deformity of the body. Wait a little, and you will see something more incredible than any wonder. For what has befallen our fluid nature does not remain forever. When the soul is set free from its entanglement with what is corruptible and earthly, then it is adorned with its own beauty. Here is the proof: after this life the man who had lived in luxury did not loathe the poor man's hand

[?] … that rich man. Yet he begged that the poor man's finger, once so diseased, might serve him then as the bearer of a drop of water, and he longed to lick with his own tongue the moisture on the poor man's finger. He would not have longed for this if he had seen the body's repulsiveness in the character of the soul. How many things the rich man must have recanted in vain once his life had changed! How often he must have called the poor man blessed for his misfortune in this life! How often he must have blamed his own lot, as one assigned wealth to the ruin of his soul! And if he could have come back to life, among whom would he have chosen to be born? Among those who prosper in this life, or among those who suffer misfortune? Clearly he would have preferred the lot of the unfortunate. For he asks that someone from the dead should go and warn his brothers, so that they too, harmed by the arrogance of wealth, should not be carried down in the luxury of the flesh into the same chasm of Hades, slipping on the smooth path of pleasure. Why, then, are we not brought to our senses by stories like these? Why do we not take up the good trade that the divine Apostle advises? "Your abundance," he says, "for their need," so that the surplus of their relief may in the life to come be enough for your salvation too. If, then, we want to receive something good, let us give first. If we want to be refreshed hereafter, let us give rest to others now. If we want them to receive us into the eternal tents, let us now receive them into ours. If we want the wounds of our sins healed, let us do the same for the bodies of the afflicted. For "blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy." But perhaps someone will say that the commandment is good for later on, but for now he is very wary of catching the disease and sharing in it. So that nothing unwanted happens to him, he thinks he must avoid going near such people. These are mere words and pretexts and fictions, specious screens for laziness about God's commandments. The truth is not like that. No danger lies hidden in carrying out the commandment. Let no one cure one evil with another. How many people can be seen, from youth to old age, devoting themselves to caring for these sufferers, and through this zeal they have not dimmed their body's natural good health at all! Nor is it likely that it should. Some diseases, such as plagues and others that depend on an outside cause, arise from tainted air or water, and most people suspect that they pass from those already seized to those who come near them. But even there, I think, the disease does not make the healthy person ill by transmission. Rather, the common onslaught brings on a similar illness, and so the disease got the reputation of passing from those already seized to the rest. But in this case, since the disease takes shape

from within, and the blood suffers a kind of corruption when destructive humours seep into it, the disease is confined to the person who has it. That this is so can also be learned from the following. Is any share of their better condition passed from the healthy to the sick, however diligently they keep up their care of them? It is not. So it is likely that the reverse holds too, and the disease does not pass from the sick to the healthy. If, then, the gain from the commandment is so great that the kingdom of heaven is prepared through it, and no harm comes to the body of the one who cares for them, what is left to keep the commandment of love from being put into practice? But do you say it is hard to force the constitution of most people, which by nature loathes such things? Very well, I agree with the statement that it is hard. But what other thing achieved by virtue can you show me that costs no toil? The law has laid down much sweat and toil for the hope of heaven. It has shown people that the road to life is hard to travel, and has walled it in on every side with toilsome and rougher ways of living. "For narrow and hard," it says, "is the way that leads to life." What then? Shall we neglect that hope of good things because it cannot be gained with ease? Let us ask the young whether self-control does not seem toilsome to them, and whether indulging their desires shamelessly is not far more desirable than a life of restraint. Shall we, then, cling to what is pleasant and easy for that reason, and shrink from the roughness of virtue? That is not the view of the Lawgiver of life, who forbade us the broad, downhill, spacious road through life. "Enter," he says, "by the narrow and hard way." So here too let us count this among the things achieved through toil: to make a habit of the commandment, which is now a stranger to our life. And let us cure the natural aversion of the healthy by persisting in the practice. For habit is powerful, and through persistence it can produce a kind of pleasure even in things that seem most difficult. So let no one say that it is toilsome. Let him say rather that what is achieved is a benefit to those who pursue it. And since the gain is great, we must think little of the toil for the sake of the gain. In time, through habit, what was toilsome for a while will become pleasant. And this too should be added to what has been said: even in this present life, compassion for the unfortunate benefits the healthy. To sensible people it is a fine thing to lay up mercy beforehand as a contribution, in the midst of other people's misfortunes. For all humankind is governed by one nature, and no one has within himself any firm pledge of lasting prosperity. So we must always remember the Gospel

precept that advises us to do for others whatever we want people to do for us. So while you are sailing in fair weather, stretch out your hand to the one who has been shipwrecked. The sea is common to all, and so are the storm and the turmoil of the waves. Reefs, rocks and crags, and all the other causes of shipwreck in life threaten everyone who sails with equal fear. While you are unharmed, while you sail the sea of life without danger, do not pass by the one who has run aground without pity. Who guarantees you fair sailing for ever? You have not yet put in to the harbour of rest. You are not yet beyond the waves. Your life has not yet set foot on solid ground. You are still being carried across the open sea of life. As you show yourself to the one who has met misfortune, so you will make your fellow voyagers toward you. But may we all reach the harbour of rest, carried through the voyage of life before us in fair weather by the Holy Spirit. May we have the practice of the commandments, and love as our rudder. Steered by these, may we reach the land of promise, where the great city stands, whose architect and builder is our God. To him be glory and power to the ages of ages. Amen.
